articles.title: College students tackle invasive plants in Worcester
articles.text:
College students tackle invasive plants in Worcester | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Ailanthus altissima, the tree-of-heaven (Courtesy Peter Del Tredici)
Clark University and the city of Worcester are teaming up to fight invasive plants.
A new program will train students to map aggressive, weedy plant species that damage Worcester’s parks, roads and public spaces.
The project is part of a larger initiative to address some of Worcester’s most consequential challenges while helping students build professional skills, according to city officials.
Mature knotweed bushes line a bicycle path on the banks for the Charles River. (Robin Lubbock/WBUR)
Students in the program will focus on three invasive plants to start — Tree of Heaven, Oriental Bittersweet and Japanese Knotweed — and try to discern where they're causing the most trouble.
“Part of that will be working with the public,” said Laurie Ross, an associate provost at Clark. “Where do complaints come in? Are they our bigger parks? Are they the schools? Are they the roadways and sidewalks? Those are the kinds of spaces.”
Once students identify the areas with the highest impact, said Ross, they’ll work with the city to determine the best course of action. This may include removing invasive plants and replacing them with local species, or educating residents on how to spot noxious weeds and stop their spread.
“The public needs to know what these things look like and how to get rid of them, “ Ross said.
The preserved remains of an Asian Longhorned Beetle in Worcester, Mass. (AP)
The new program will complement Clark's existing research on invasive species in Worcester. For more than a decade, students and faculty have studied a devastating infestation of Asian long-horned beetles, which forced the city to remove 30,000 trees.
It's also the second partnership Clark and Worcester have formalized this fall. In September, the city and the university created a program to improve pathways to college for Worcester students.
“Partnerships like this can help tackle real issues that are affecting the city and its residents,” said Worcester City Manager Eric Batista in a statement, “while giving experiential learning opportunities to college students.”

articles.title: Lanternflies are creeping into Mass. Here's why you should kill them
articles.text:
Lanternflies are creeping into Mass. Here's why you should kill them | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
A spotted lanternfly at a vineyard in Kutztown, Pennsylvania. (Matt Rourke/AP)
A new infestation of the pesky spotted lanternfly was discovered in Holyoke in late August, according to the Massachusetts Department of Agricultural Resources.
Holyoke is now one of a handful of cities and towns in Massachusetts contending with the invasive species that officials say should be squashed on sight. The colorful pests seem to be spreading in the state, and they can cause significant damage to fruit crops and other trees.
The new infestation is yet to be added to the department's  maps charting lanternfly populations in the state. The agency issued an alert about the infestation in early September, notifying Holyoke residents that surveyors will check area trees for the bugs and that locals should report any sightings of them.
The discovery shows the bugs have spread around the state since the first individual lanternfly was found in Massachusetts in 2018, said Jennifer Forman Orth, a biologist with the agriculture department.
In addition to Holyoke, Springfield, Fitchburg, Shrewsbury and Worcester each face known infestations. (An infestation is defined either by multiple insects congregating or by discovering egg masses.) Individual lanternflies have been found across the state from Berkshire County to Boston — and even on Martha's Vineyard.
The lanternfly is about an inch long, with black-spotted wings and smaller, bright red underwings. And the species can cause a lot of agricultural problems.
Lanternflies eat sap inside trees or plants by jabbing their straw-like mouthpieces into tree trunks or plant stems. Their plant of choice is the tree of heaven (which is an invasive species as well), but they'll feast on other important New England trees and crops, including apple trees, grape vines, maple trees and hops. Their feeding habits damage plants and ultimately lead to crop loss.
When they feed, spotted lanternflies excrete a sticky, sap-like substance called honeydew that collects on surfaces, eventually fermenting and growing a smelly black substance called sooty mold fungi.
Honeydew and sooty mold fungi are not toxic to humans and won't immediately kill a plant, said Forman Orth, but the black fungi can make it harder for plants to photosynthesize and more vulnerable to outside environmental impacts.
"If there's other environmental issues going on, like drought or flooding, or some other disease, then they're potentially going to be more susceptible to that," she explained.
Lanternflies also tend to swarm together, especially in late summer, which can be a problem for businesses that rely on outdoor events.
"There's a potential impact to orchards, especially any orchards that do pick-your-own-fruit type activities where they want the public to come out and enjoy the farm and be out in nature," said Forman Orth. "In states where they have major infestations, that swarming behavior of the lanternflies can make it really difficult to enjoy the outdoors."
Spotted lanternflies gather on a tree in Kutztown, Pennsylvania. (Matt Rourke/AP)
Pennsylvania and New York are both dealing with large infestations of the pest. Officials in those states and from the U.S. Department of Agriculture are asking residents to squash the bugs whenever they get the chance. (You may have seen videos of people killing the pests on social media.)
"I think citizens are doing a great job and controlling the ones they can by stepping on them," said Brian Eshenaur, an invasive species specialist with Cornell working for the New York State Integrated Pest Management program. "They're not in every place yet, and we want to slow the spread as much as possible."
Lanternflies are originally found in China in a climate similar to that of the northeastern United States, and were first spotted in the U.S. in 2014. They lay masses of 30 to 50 eggs around late September or October. The masses are hearty enough to last through cold winters and hatch around April.
Eshenaur said it's too early to tell if the warming climate is having an impact on the species' spread, but that warmer springs could mean their eggs hatch earlier. He also noted that adults lay eggs until they die at the first hard frost, so a delayed start to the first frost because of a warmer fall season could make for a longer egg-laying season.
Spotted lanternflies are excellent hitchhikers, which is part of what makes them so difficult to contain. Despite their name, Forman Orth said they are not strong fliers, so any time they pop up in a new state or town that seems far from other infestations, it's likely they caught a ride there.
They climb onto people, clothing, wheel wells of vehicles or onto truck beds. They fly through open car windows. It's believed that the lanternfly first came to the United States on shipments of stone sent to Pennsylvania.
Eshenaur said part of the reason they're so good at hitchhiking is that spotted lanternflies are always on the move. The pests constantly need to feed and are in perpetual search for food.
He also noted that while the insect often lays its egg masses on tree bark or firewood, it can deposit eggs on nearly any surface.
"We have found that they will lay on camp chairs, on outdoor seat cushions," Eshenaur said.
If a lanternfly lays its egg mass on something that gets moved to a new location, it's possible that its eggs could hatch somewhere the species hasn't been found yet.
"If they're traveling on a vehicle or a shipment of wood or anything like that, then there's no finite limit to the amount of miles they can go. And that makes it very challenging to predict," said Forman Orth.
A spotted lanternfly nymph climbs the leg of Pennsylvania state Sen. Vincent Hughes during a 2021 rally in Philadelphia. (Matt Slocum/AP)

articles.title: Native groups seek to repair lands damaged by colonization
articles.text:
Native groups seek to repair lands damaged by colonization | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Fin Jones, of Falmouth and a member of the Mashpee Wampanoag tribe, top center, and Jessica Tran, right, of St. Paul, Minn., work to remove invasive plant species at the Wampanoag Common Lands project, in Kingston, Aug. 2. (Steven Senne/AP)
Asa Peters marched into a thicket of Japanese knotweed in the woods of coastal Massachusetts this month and began steadily hacking the towering, dense vegetation down to size.
The 24-year-old member of the Mashpee Wampanoag tribe was among a cadre of volunteers rooting out invasive species and tending to recently planted native vegetation on a wide swath of forest acquired on behalf of his federally recognized tribe and other Wampanoag communities.
“It’s hard. You got to keep pulling and pulling. Starting to really sweat, but it’s cool,” he said as he took a quick break in the sweltering August heat. “We’re in the early stages, putting in the work to create a special place where we can do all kinds of great things.”
The Wampanoag Common Lands, as the project is called, seeks to restore a 32-acre (13-hectare) former Catholic summer camp on the banks of the Muddy Pond in Kingston to something closer to what it might have looked like before European colonization transformed it.
The Native Land Conservancy, the local Native group that received the donated land this year, envisions a natural environment filled with indigenous plants and animals where Wampanoags can practice cultural ceremonies and educate new generations in traditional ways.
Ramona Peters, a Mashpee Wampanoag who founded the conservancy, said the effort is all the more meaningful because the land is some 5 miles from where Pilgrims arriving on the Mayflower established the English colony of Plymouth, near the remnants of a Wampanoag community wiped out by European disease.
“This is basically where the first impact of colonization of this country happened,” she said. “It’s very significant that it’s been returned to us.”
The Wampanoag Common Lands is part of a growing movement of Indigenous-led conservation efforts helping to preserve and reinvigorate Native culture and identity, said Beth Rose-Middleton, a professor at the University of California, Davis, focused on Native American environmental policy and conservation.
The efforts are also critical in the face of climate change, which has acutely harmed Native communities, she said. Alaska tribes facing increased erosion, flooding and thawing permafrost have weighed relocating from their coastal and riverside lands. Louisiana bayou tribes still reeling from Hurricane Ida last year are bracing for ever-powerful storms, while across the American West, tribes are contending with a historic drought that has upended their way of life.
“Many of our land and waterscapes have been pressed into extreme uses and depleted,” Rose-Middletown said. “Land stewardship and care work are necessary for creating resilient landscapes.”
In northern California, the Wiyot Tribe has spent more than two decades restoring a badly polluted island that was the site of an 1860 massacre that nearly wiped out the tribe and, more recently, was home to a ship repair facility.
Michelle Vassel, the tribe’s administrator, said the years of environmental work on Tuluwat have contributed to better water quality and marine habitats across Humboldt Bay.
“For us, it’s a responsibility. Indigenous people are tied to a place,” she said. “This work is also healing. The history of the massacre has always been a scar on the broader community. This was a way to change that history.”
Tribes in Wyoming and other Great Plains states, meanwhile, have been reintroducing bison herds brought to near-extinction by European settlers. Those in Washington state and other parts of the Pacific Northwest are focused on protecting glacial rivers vital for migrating salmon from warming waters and the effects of dams and industrial pollution.
And on the Massachusetts island of Martha’s Vineyard, the Native-run Sassafras Earth Education has been teaching youths and families traditional Wampanoag cultivation practices for decades.
The organization’s Land Culture Project seeks to transform roughly 20 acres (8 hectares) of forested land and fields into a “highly productive food forest” of native trees and shrubs beneficial to both people and wildlife.
“It’s not just about restoring the physical land,” said Saskia Vanderhoop, who founded the organization with her husband, David Vanderhoop, an Aquinnah Wampanoag elder. “It’s also about restoring the culture.”
At the nearby Wampanoag Common Lands, old summer camp buildings were torn down and pavement, athletic courts and other hard surfaces scraped away this year.
Even large, nonnative Norwegian spruce trees were uprooted by the prior owners at the conservancy’s request, leaving mostly a bare clearing near the water’s edge.
In their place, conservancy staff and volunteers this summer planted dozens of native species significant to Wampanoag culture, such as white oak trees, blueberry bushes, witch hazel, goldenrod and hay-scented ferns.
Wildlife cameras have been set up to survey and monitor otters, deer and other local fauna. The conservancy is also building bat houses and considering reintroducing threatened and rare native animal species, such as northern red-bellied turtles, said Diana Ruiz, the Native Land Conservancy’s director.
The organization is also exploring other uses, such as traditional Wampanoag lodges for hosting guests or other community functions.
“We’re not looking at it as just this closed system that humans sometimes visit,” she said. “We’re looking at it as a space where the Wampanoag community can reconnect with their ancestral homeland in an active and deep way.”
For Asa Peters, that potential for spiritual revitalization is what he finds most compelling about the land project.

articles.title: Gardening is a dose of reality
articles.text:
Gardening is a dose of reality | Cognoscenti
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
A woman in weeding a path in a vegetable garden. (Getty images)
At 72, I’ve discovered something new about myself: I hate gardening.
Until moving to a co-housing community in Western Massachusetts, I had no opportunity to explore my possible affinity for botanical pursuits. Our longtime home in Cambridge was flanked by two narrow alleys and fronted by two postage stamp-sized plots of land that held two immortal rosebushes and a riot of untended weeds that I chose to think of as simply “native plants.” Our Somerville home before that had only one alley and the only growing thing in it was the pile of garbage bags that didn’t fit into the bins. And in both homes, between working full-time and raising kids, I had no time for such frivolity.
But our new home is surrounded by grass (which yes, we’re dutifully trying to convert to other forms of less water-requiring, more pollinator-friendly ground cover). We have two large standing beds that sprout Japanese eggplants and cherry tomatoes even more numerous than the insects feasting on them. Our campus has trees, plants, flowers and a community garden — all kinds of green and yellow stuff that I’m told requires care from many hands.
Now a retiree, I am a woman free to spend my hours auditing courses in music appreciation and Middle Eastern history and psychobiography, taking my dog for long ambling walks in the woods, sleeping late and then going to water aerobics classes.
But not wanting to be a slacker, either in my home or community, I’ve signed up to do my part in tending to the land.
Now I understand why my neighbors snarl when they say “mug wort” or “Japanese knotweed” though this is only an adopted loathing.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, it’s the weeding that does me in. I despise the kneeling, bending, digging, tugging futility of it all. Now I understand why my neighbors snarl when they say “mug wort” or “Japanese knotweed” though this is only an adopted loathing. These plants look no better or worse to me than the milkweed or golden rod that I’m supposed to love, and they have a stubborn indifference to my labor that I find almost admirable.
That’s why as I squat and stab the dirt with my trowel, I wonder why I’ve singled out weeding as the target of my loathing. After all, I engage in plenty of endlessly recurring activities in the course of daily life. Many, like vacuuming up dog hair or emptying and reloading the dishwasher, don’t arouse antipathy so much as a kind of spiritual fatigue. And some, like folding laundry or making the bed feel not only satisfying, but comforting. The warmth of the clothes newly emerged from the dryer, the precision of a well-aligned top sheet, arouse not only a mild sensory pleasure but a transient belief that I have control over at least some aspects of my life.
Creeping Wood Sorrel and Purple Deadnettle strangle that illusion. The weeds are relentless, and after an hour (or at least what feels like an hour) of extracting them leaves me with a stiff back, aching knees, and tired arms.
But ultimately, that’s why I’m motivated to do this tedious, unrewarding task. It scares me a little to think that I no longer need to work, and terrifies me to think that I’m no longer capable of it.
I am a woman of relative leisure now in my retirement. And leisure, however well-earned, breeds obliviousness to the lives of others. I fear the prospect of losing my appreciation for the people landscaping other my neighbors’ lawns, for those paving roads and washing dishes for eight hours a day. I’m afraid I’ll even stop noticing them unless my back aches a little too, not just from age but from labor. There’s a reason why Marge Piercy’s poem, “ To Be of Use,” has hung next to every desk I’ve ever worked at. Living solely to satisfy myself feels, well, self-satisfied.
It scares me a little to think that I no longer need to work, and terrifies me to think that I’m no longer capable of it.
And to be fair, I don’t hate everything about my land-tending duties.
Mowing is okay — noisy but gratifying. Turning the compost, though stinky, offers a dynamic lesson in transformation. Egg shells, orange peels and slimy cilantro become nutrients that literally steam in the cool morning air. And when the occasional startled squirrel leaps out of the compost bin, I feel a novel solidarity in our brief moment of shared terror.
Pruning the yellow grass-spheres outside the garbage shed also offers a few unexpected rewards. The plants’ spiky straw shoots remind me of the brush cut worn by Mr. Blanchard, the brute of an algebra teacher I had in 9th grade, the man whose first love was coaching the football team (sine, cosine, hup!) and second love was throwing erasers at students like me for failing to comprehend the staccato bursts of what he claimed was explanation. In what feels like belated revenge, I love snapping the giant gardening shears at this stand-in for Mr. Blanchard’s scalp, slicing through these quills with all the force my growing triceps can muster.
As I write these words, I see the violence in my language about pruning and weeding — the stabbing and yanking and decapitating of poor dandelions. But the plants survive my aggression, maybe even prosper in the long run because of it. And though this may be naïve, in this era of climate crisis I find solace in that fact.
I can’t envision gardening ever being a hobby, let alone a passion, as I know it is for many other people. But it’s a dose of reality, a necessary grounding in an otherwise privileged life. Digging in the dirt keeps me connected, both to the tenacity of the natural world and to the lives of others.

articles.title: Our favorite local music we heard in November
articles.text:
Our favorite local music we heard in November | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Album covers, clockwise from top left: SuperSmashBroz’s “Global Entry” (Courtesy Rashon Sloan); Magen Tracy & The Missed Connections’ “Taking Me Longer” (Courtesy Jill McCracken); Charles Overton’s “Reflections” (Photo by Adama Jalloh, design by Studio Torsten Posselt); Errol Strength’s “Love Flavor” (Courtesy Jack Dalrymple); and Cloudbelly’s “Throwing the Game” (Courtesy Bob Krzykowksi).
An album brimming with sensitive songs and euphoric arrangements. A debut EP from a creative harpist and composer. The latest album from a DJ/producer duo of brothers with international influences. Plus, a reggae single that captures the wonder of newly rekindled romance and a hopeful song that examines the hardships and resilience of life. WBUR music critics share the latest songs that caught their ears this month.
Cloudbelly, ' Throwing the Game'
I first discovered Cloudbelly through their submissions to NPR’s Tiny Desk Contest. The band is fronted by singer-songwriter Corey Laitman, whose yearning, poetic ruminations are well served by a stripped-down Tiny Desk treatment. But a studio album is a different kind of endeavor. The group’s latest LP, “Throwing the Game,” presents Laitman’s sensitive songs inside euphoric arrangements, layering synths and strings to cinematic effect. The best treatments allow in some grit and playfulness, like the scuffed guitar solo in “Oh, Antarctica!” or the mischievous dialogue between guitar and bass in “Charlie.” Similarly, the most effective songs allow sharp specificity to sit alongside more abstract lyrics. My favorite is “Vampires (Wolves),” a nostalgic portrait of an early romance, which features bracing lines like “I fumble a dildo/ And you take me into bed” alongside more impressionistic images: “We rang out like bells/ Until somebody overheard.” The song crescendos and then abruptly ends, Laitman’s voice ringing out clear on the final ambivalent lines. It’s a song with the texture of a memory that offers insight into the past but no tidy conclusions — precisely the kind of songwriting at which “Throwing the Game” excels. — Amelia Mason
Charles Overton, ' Reflections'
In recent years, a small group of musicians has changed the perception of the harp by bringing the instrument into modern jazz, folk and new music contexts. Among them is Boston’s Charles Overton. His penchant for creativity has led to tours of the elite festival circuit with British flautist Shabaka Hutchings and devotional singer-songwriter (and Harvard Ph.D.) Ganavya, while his virtuosity means he routinely performs with the Boston Symphony Orchestra, Boston Pops and Boston Ballet.
So it’s rather shocking to discover that he’s only now releasing his debut EP. “Reflections” was born when the German label LEITER suggested the harpist go into their studio while he was touring with Ganavya. From the first notes of the opening “Tomorrow,” the listener hears how Overton uses improvisation to bring out unexpected sonic textures and a thoughtful arc. The second track, “Rumination,” introduces the only other musician on the record: Berlin drummer Hiromu Seifert, whose rhythmic inventions add another layer of meaning to the five-track EP. While the beginning of “Dawn” hints at the piece’s origin — a composition Overton made for an online meditation series — the friction between the harp and the drums makes this music that is as exciting as it is contemplative. — Noah Schaffer
Charles Overton celebrates the release of “Reflections” on Dec. 4 at the Jazz Urbane Cafe in Roxbury.
Magen Tracy & the Missed Connections, ' Taking Me Longer'
Boston-area band Magen Tracy & the Missed Connections explore a variety of sounds from alt-country and Americana to lively pop and rock. Their latest single “Taking Me Longer” opens with a brash riff laced with lighter, hopeful fingerpicking. Drawing from Fleetwood Mac, the track feels wistful and mysterious. Frontwoman Magen Tracy examines life’s hardships and the resilience that emerges from conquering them. She sings, “I’ll be the better man/ Run as fast as I can/ Till it’s over, cuz first I got sober/ And then I got stronger/ It’s just taking me longer.” The initial idea for the track came from Tracy observing her friend navigating a breakup. As she came apart, she also built herself back stronger and wiser. “Taking Me Longer” is a reminder that even when dark situations feel impossible to escape, we can find a way out and grow in the process. — Maddie Browning
SuperSmashBroz, ' Global Entry'
Even though U.S. flights experienced a major ground stop this month, Boston’s SuperSmashBroz made sure we received “Global Entry.” Nothing would stop them from helping you “Get Your Vibes Right,” which is the motto of their career. The DJ/producer brother duo put out a nine-song Afrobeats project that has had me moving and grooving since I first got to experience it. They collaborated with multiple other producers, and the vocalists on the project come from all over: Massachusetts, California, the Netherlands, Canada, Ghana.
“Relocate” is a standout: Nonso Amadi and Kkeda trade verses over a feel-good, flirty music bed. It’s the kind of track that would play during the ending moments of a great date night. That tension two lovers feel and can’t escape. A lot of Afrobeats sequencing is meant to activate the footwork specialist in the most laid-back party-goer. The more upbeat groove crafting in “Luvaman,” “Can We Go,” “Tongue Tied,” “Gara (No Wahala)” and “Shut It Down” gets that job done. (But “Can We Go” wins my top choice.) Lead single “Coconut Water” gives the listener a great range of vibes to choose from, including hip-hop, even with Afrobeats being the main character. What I like the most about the brothers’ latest catalog additions is the fact that DJing continues to be the root of their growth. — Noble

articles.title: 6 holiday shows to see this season
articles.text:
6 holiday shows to see this season | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
The cast of Commonwealth Shakespeare Company’s “A Christmas Carol.” (Courtesy Nile Scott Studios)
There’s something about the holiday season that brings out the wonder in us all. Several theater makers are offering warm and fuzzy classic tales such as “A Christmas Carol,” but there are also a few alternatives offering comedy, a smidge of horror and a dash of drag. Here are six productions to consider this holiday season.
' A Christmas for the Birds'
Iron Wolf Theatre | Nov. 27-Dec. 20
Alfred Hitchcock’s 1963 horror film “The Birds” gets a makeover from the Gold Dust Orphans for their annual holiday show. In Hitchcock’s film, an adaptation of Daphne du Maurier’s 1952 short story of the same name, a socialite named Melanie Daniels heads to Bodega Bay with attorney Mitch Brenner. However, the trip takes a frightening turn when the town is subjected to the escalating attacks by flocks of birds.
In the Gold Dust Orphans version written by Ryan Landry, Melanie Daniels and Mitch Brenner’s meet-cute is in Boston at a bird shop. Later, Melanie heads to Provincetown to meet him and his sister and brings along two turtledoves as a prank. But their sweet holiday trip turns frightening when more than 6,500 birds show up to wreak havoc. If their previous productions give any hint to what’s in store, there will be props galore, extravagant costume changes, music and lots of laughter, not to mention a deeper moral message in the text. The show is being staged at the Iron Wolf Theatre at South Boston Lithuanian Citizens’ Association.
Maddie Hatton as Melanie Daniels and Evan Turissini as Mitch Brenner in the Gold Dust Orphans’ “A Christmas for the Birds.” (Courtesy Michael von Redlich)
' Sister's Christmas Catechism: The Mystery of the Magi's Gold'
Charles Playhouse | Nov. 27-Jan. 3
Writers Vicki Quade and Maripat Donovan put their experiences growing up Catholic and school stories from families and friends into a one-woman show called “Late Night Catechism,” first produced in 1993. Since then, the show’s popularity — it’s considered the longest-running religious comedy in Chicago’s history, according to Broadway World — prompted follow-ups. One of those shows is “Sister’s Christmas Catechism: The Mystery of the Magi’s Gold,” written by Donovan along with Marc Silvia and Jane Morris. In the interactive show, the audience is the class, and Sister leads a “CSI: Bethlehem” style investigation exploring what happened to the Magi’s gold. There will be pop quizzes, reprimands and more.
' The Jinkx & DeLa Holiday Show'
Boch Center Wang Theatre | Nov. 28
For the last nine years, award-winning comedians, writers, actors and drag queens BenDeLaCreme and Jinkx Monsoon of “RuPaul’s Drag Race” fame have hosted their popular holiday show. Along the way, the two have “met sentient Christmas treats, twisted space-time with Dickensian Ghosts, ventured to the Nutcracker's Land of Sweets, as well as survived immaculate conceptions, AI, body swaps, and elf attacks,” according to the show’s description. This year’s installment is written and directed by BenDeLaCreme with additional writing by Jinkx Monsoon. While details of the hijinks have yet to be unveiled, there will be music, dancing and holiday cheer.
BenDeLaCreme and Jinkx Monsoon (Courtesy Magnus Hastings, design by Brendan Haley)
' ChristmasTime'
Robinson Theatre | Dec. 5-13
Each year the Reagle Music Theatre of Greater Boston pulls out all the stops for its  “ChristmasTime” production in Waltham. The cast of more than 100 and a live orchestra perform holiday tunes and recreate multiple holiday scenes, including a voyage to the North Pole, a living Nativity scene and a glimpse of a Victorian Christmas aimed at entertaining adults and children.
' A Christmas Carol'
Emerson Cutler Majestic Theatre | Dec. 11-20
There are few holiday tales as enduring as Charles Dickens’ 1843 novella “A Christmas Carol,” where an elderly man with a sour disposition learns what’s important in life after he receives visits from three ghosts. Set in early Victorian England, Commonwealth Shakespeare Company’s story of redemption is an adaptation by award-winning writer and Steve Wargo. With beautiful traditional 19th-century carols arranged by Dianne Adams McDowell, the show has become a Greater Boston tradition. CSC’s founding artistic director Steven Maler will direct the show and Dan Rodriguez provides musical direction.
Will Lyman and Damon Singletary in Commonwealth Shakespeare Company’s “A Christmas Carol.” (Courtesy Nile Scott Studios)
If you live outside of the city, don’t fret; there’s likely “A Christmas Carol” near you. In Worcester, the Hanover Theatre & Conservatory’s production has been reimagined by acclaimed Broadway director Billie Aken-Tyers and runs Dec. 17-23. In Providence, Trinity Rep’s show directed by Taavon Gamble is onstage now and runs through Dec. 31. Over in Beverly, North Shore Music Theatre’s show directed by Kevin P. Hill runs Dec. 3-23. And Berkshire Theatre Group’s rendition, directed by David Adkins and Isadora Wolfe, runs Dec. 3-20 in Stockbridge.
' Holiday Feast'
Modern Theatre at Suffolk University | Dec. 19-20
The Front Porch Arts Collective aims to bring the community together with laughter for its annual “Holiday Feast,” serving up a taste of Black sitcoms performed live. This year, the cast will perform the 1995 episode “Let It Snow, Let It Snow, Let It Snow…Dammit” of “Living Single,” where beloved handyman Overton invites his friends to his family cabin for Christmas and attempts to recreate his childhood traditions. Next, a more Scrooge-like lesson is learned in the 1998 “Christmas Day-Ja Vu” episode of “The Jamie Foxx Show,” where the central character Jamie buys himself gifts instead of for his loved ones. articles.text:
Chef and restaurateur on reclaiming Indigenous foods and traditions | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Most of food we eat in the U.S. isn't native to this region. That realization hit chef Sean Sherman hard — and transformed his cooking. Sherman, who grew up in a Lakota reservation in South Dakota, is one of the foremost voices in the Indigenous food movement.
"If we want to really celebrate indigeneity, then we should be buying foods from Indigenous producers and making Indigenous recipes and making foods that taste like where we are," Sherman said.
Sherman is now a Minneapolis-based restaurateur and the author of "Turtle Island: Foods and Traditions of the Indigenous Peoples of North America."
This segment aired on November 26, 2026.

articles.title: Boston to open new all-electric public library in Fields Corner
articles.text:
Boston to open new all-electric public library in Fields Corner | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Dorchester’s new $30.9 million Fields Corner branch of the Boston Public Library is an all-electric, fossil fuel-free building designed to meet the city’s Zero Net Carbon standard for municipal buildings. It will open to the public on Dec. 12. (Courtesy Dorchester Reporter)
Dorchester’s new Fields Corner branch of the Boston Public Library will open to the public on Sat., Dec. 12, with a ribbon-cutting ceremony at 10 a.m.
The new $30.9 million, two-story, 14,790-square-foot building replaces the previous branch that opened in 1969 at the intersection of Park Street and Dorchester Avenue.
The new library will house an expanded collection of nearly 33,000 volumes, a flexible 100-seat community meeting room, a 20-person classroom, two study rooms, and dedicated spaces for children, teens, and adults.
Other amenities include a second-floor outdoor reading terrace, public computers, laptops, a printing station, and a children’s story area with a custom reading nook.
As t he Reporter detailed last December, the new building has an important design distinction: Its superstructure is framed with glulams, or engineered wood, instead of conventional steel beams. The exposed, light-colored wooden beams suggest the feel of a cabin or ski lodge and are a prominent feature of the finished interior.
The Fields Corner branch is the first in the BPL system to employ the construction technique, which is part of a broader “mass timber” movement that promotes sustainable alternatives to steel and concrete construction.
Evan Brinkman, assistant director of design for the city’s Public Facilities Department, told the Reporter last year that the Fields Corner project was notable for its use of “wood more extensively, not only for the primary frame, but also for the floor slabs and wall framing.”
Residents helped shape the design through six public meetings, including one focused specifically on sustainability. The all-electric, fossil fuel-free building was designed to meet the city’s Zero Net Carbon standard for municipal buildings and is targeting LEED Gold certification. Its roof is designed to accommodate solar panels in the future.
The Fields Corner branch will be open Mondays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.; Tuesdays from noon to 8 p.m.; and Fridays and Saturdays from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.
